papers.title: Myocardial injury with non-obstructive coronary arteries: diagnostic pathways and stratified treatment.
papers.short_title: a review of MINOCA diagnostic pathways and stratified treatment
papers.summary: In this Lancet Review, Rocco Montone, Roxana Mehran and Filippo Crea examine myocardial injury with non-obstructive coronary arteries, or MINOCA. They argue that MINOCA challenges the long-standing assumption that myocardial infarction is synonymous with obstructive coronary disease, and that rather than a paradox it reflects the limits of angiography-centred thinking. The review treats MINOCA as a working diagnosis covering diverse mechanisms: plaque disruption, coronary vasomotor dysfunction, microvascular disease and non-coronary conditions. The authors propose a pragmatic, mechanism-oriented framework for selecting and sequencing investigations, integrating intracoronary imaging, cardiac magnetic resonance and coronary functional testing according to the clinical scenario, while balancing diagnostic yield against procedural risk and resource availability. Treatment, they argue, should be guided by the underlying pathophysiology rather than a uniform approach borrowed from obstructive infarction, and emerging evidence supports stratified therapy to improve patient-centred outcomes. They close with research priorities toward a mechanism-based taxonomy. As a narrative review, the abstract reports no numerical results.
papers.critique: Strongest: a clear, clinically usable framework from leading authors that tells the cath lab team when to add optical coherence tomography, functional testing and cardiac MRI, rather than stopping at a normal-looking angiogram. Weakest: it is a narrative review whose abstract describes no systematic search or pooled data, and the authors' university press release says it synthesises the team's own earlier studies, citing their PROMISE trial as validation. TCTMD's related coverage of PROMISE reported better angina-related health status but noted early termination, only 100 patients and no blinding, so benefit on hard endpoints remains unproven. No independent commentary on this paper was found yet.

papers.title: Antithrombotic Therapy After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting.
papers.summary: From Galli, Angiolillo and an international group of cardiologists and cardiac surgeons, this Special Communication reviews antithrombotic therapy as secondary prevention after coronary artery bypass grafting. Bypass surgery remains the cornerstone of revascularisation in complex coronary disease, but long-term outcomes are limited by graft failure, particularly of saphenous vein grafts, and by recurrent ischaemic events. Graft attrition is time dependent: early failure is driven mainly by platelet-mediated thrombosis, and later failure by intimal hyperplasia and accelerated atherosclerosis, so antithrombotic therapy needs a time-adapted approach. Lifelong aspirin remains the foundation, whereas the intensity and duration of dual antiplatelet therapy remain controversial. Strategies have historically been extrapolated from PCI, despite differences in the pathophysiology of ischaemic recurrence and in bleeding risk. As PCI has moved toward risk-adapted and de-escalation strategies, emerging surgery-specific randomised trials are challenging routine PCI-like dual antiplatelet therapy. The review proposes a risk-adapted framework integrating graft-failure pathophysiology, clinical presentation and bleeding susceptibility. Its abstract reports no numerical results.
papers.critique: Strongest: a multidisciplinary author group spanning interventional cardiology, pharmacology and cardiac surgery, and a mechanistic, time-dependent view of graft failure that moves beyond simply copying PCI regimens. Weakest: it is a narrative expert review with no systematic search or pooled estimates in its abstract, so its framework rests on judgement and a small number of surgery-specific trials. TCTMD's related coverage of TACSI and TOP-CABG shows that evidence: a year of ticagrelor plus aspirin doubled major bleeding without reducing events, while three-month de-escalation kept vein graft patency, though it is unproven that fewer occlusions mean fewer hard events. No independent commentary on this paper was found yet.

papers.title: Blood-Pressure-Lowering Treatment across the Cardiovascular Risk Spectrum.
papers.short_title: blood-pressure lowering across the cardiovascular risk spectrum
papers.summary: This individual-participant meta-analysis pooled 51 randomised trials with 357,440 participants followed for a median 4.2 years. Each 5 mm Hg systolic reduction lowered major cardiovascular events, hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.88 to 0.92, with no variation across ten predicted-risk deciles, including five-year risk below 4%. Absolute five-year benefit was 2.6 versus 0.4 percentage points in the highest versus lowest decile, numbers needed to treat 38 versus 255. Hypotension-type, renal and fall-related adverse events rose modestly.
papers.study_type: Individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised trials
papers.relevance: Supports treating blood pressure in lower-risk as well as post-PCI patients, with the absolute gain scaling with baseline risk.

papers.title: Computed Tomography Imaging Markers Associated With Prognosis at 10 Years: A Post Hoc Analysis of the SCOT-HEART Randomized Clinical Trial.
papers.short_title: ten-year prognosis from CT plaque markers in SCOT-HEART
papers.summary: This post hoc analysis of the SCOT-HEART trial studied 1,769 patients with stable chest pain who had coronary CT angiography at three Scottish centres. Over 10 years, 117, or 6.6%, had myocardial infarction or coronary death. After adjustment for risk score and scanner, total, calcified, noncalcified and low-attenuation plaque burdens each predicted events; per doubling of low-attenuation plaque the hazard ratio was 1.51, 95% CI 1.28 to 1.78. Low-attenuation plaque burden above 4% carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.66.
papers.study_type: Post hoc analysis of a randomised trial
papers.relevance: Relevant to CT-first chest pain pathways in Ireland and the UK, where quantitative plaque metrics may sharpen who needs invasive assessment or intensive prevention.

papers.title: Aortic Sclerosis and Aortic Stenosis: Two Entities or a Continuum?
papers.short_title: aortic sclerosis and stenosis as one continuum
papers.summary: This retrospective study analysed 181,167 adults with morphologically abnormal aortic valves and peak transvalvular velocity of 1.0 to 3.9 m/s on echocardiography between 2010 and 2022, excluding severe stenosis. Over a median 3.2 years, 4,112 underwent valve replacement and 61,654 died. Replacement risk rose gradually across the velocity range with no threshold separating sclerosis from stenosis; five-year incidence rose from 0.1% at 1.0 to 1.4 m/s to 31.2% at 3.0 to 3.9 m/s. Associations with mortality persisted after adjustment.
papers.relevance: Argues for surveillance of valves labelled merely sclerotic, since they feed the future TAVI pipeline.

papers.title: Center Performance Assessment in Congenital Heart Surgery Is Method Dependent.
papers.short_title: method-dependent centre ratings in congenital heart surgery
papers.summary: Using 42,579 benchmark operations at 115 centres in the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Congenital Heart Surgery Database from 2016 to 2022, this study compared conventional regression with three causal weighting methods for estimating observed-to-expected operative mortality. Unadjusted mortality was 2.37%. Weighting estimates were higher and more variable, classifying 13.9% to 20% of centres as having higher than expected mortality, versus 7.8% with regression. The same centre could receive different ratings purely because of the statistical method.
papers.relevance: Limited direct relevance, but a caution for any centre-level outcome league tables, including PCI and TAVI registries.

papers.title: Process, Heterogeneity, and Modifiable Risk Factors of Postoperative Recovery After Cardiac Surgery.
papers.summary: This prospective cohort enrolled 2,993 patients having non-emergent cardiac surgery at eight Chinese centres in 2023 and 2024, tracking the nine-item Fuwai-Cardiac Recovery Scale from baseline to three months. A total score of 30 or less was reached by 77.4% at discharge and 97.7% at three months. Thirst, toileting dependency and poor mobility dominated early symptom burden. Three poor-recovery patterns emerged, linked to modifiable factors such as smoking, obesity and anaemia; anaemia and poor appetite, odds ratio 1.47.
papers.relevance: Mainly of cardiac surgical interest, though useful when counselling patients weighing surgery against transcatheter options.
